name: Written in Our Cells: From Mendel's Peas to CRISPR
description: How we learned what is passed from parent to child, found it written in DNA, read the whole human text, and learned to edit it.

checkpoints.name: Peas and cells
checkpoints.note: The microscope reveals cells, and cell theory holds that all life is made of them. Lamarckism says creatures pass on traits they acquire, and Charles Darwin's natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species, lacks a way to explain heredity. In 1866 Gregor Mendel shows with peas that traits pass on in fixed ratios, and is ignored.

checkpoints.name: Genes on chromosomes
checkpoints.note: In 1900 three botanists find Mendel's work again, and Mendelian inheritance becomes the base of a new science named genetics. Lamarckism fades. Studying maize, Barbara McClintock links visible traits to changes in chromosomes and finds that some genes can move from place to place.

checkpoints.name: The double helix
checkpoints.note: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images of DNA help James Watson and Francis Crick build their model of the double helix in 1953. It shows how a molecule can carry and copy a code. Crick goes on to help crack how genes are read, and Watson and Crick share a Nobel Prize in 1962, four years after Franklin's death.

checkpoints.name: Engineering life
checkpoints.note: Scientists learn to move genes between species, and in 1982 human insulin made by engineered bacteria becomes the first such medicine. McClintock wins a Nobel Prize in 1983. The Human Genome Project begins in 1990, the Flavr Savr tomato is the first engineered food on sale, and Dolly the sheep is cloned from an adult cell.

checkpoints.name: Reading and rewriting
checkpoints.note: The human genome is declared complete in 2003. Ancient DNA shows that our ancestors met Neanderthals and Denisovans and left with some of their genes. Jennifer Doudna helps turn CRISPR into a gene editor, and the genome of the COVID-19 virus, shared within weeks, guides the first mRNA vaccines.
